examples.question_text: Describe $-2\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $3\underset{\sim}{j}$ as movements, and state their magnitudes. State the angle between the horizontal and vertical directions.

examples.solution_text:
$|\underset{\sim}{p}|=1$ and $|\underset{\sim}{q}|=1$: each arrow spans one square. Both are unit vectors, although they point in different directions.

$|\underset{\sim}{r}|=3$, so $\underset{\sim}{r}$ is not a unit vector.

examples.question_text: Vector $\underset{\sim}{u}$ points south-east and has magnitude $1$. Vector $\underset{\sim}{v}$ points west and has magnitude $0.6$. State whether each is a unit vector.
examples.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{u}$ is a unit vector because $|\underset{\sim}{u}|=1$.

$\underset{\sim}{v}$ is not a unit vector because $|\underset{\sim}{v}|=0.6$.

A unit vector must have magnitude exactly $1$; its direction does not affect this test.

examples.question_text: Vector $\underset{\sim}{z}$ has magnitude $0$. Name the vector, state whether it is a unit vector, and describe its direction.
examples.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{z}=\underset{\sim}{0}$, the zero vector.

It is not a unit vector because its magnitude is $0$, rather than $1$. It has no direction.

examples.question_text:
(a) Simplify $8\underset{\sim}{c}-8\underset{\sim}{c}$.

(b) A walker travels $4$ km north from a shelter, then returns along the same route. State the displacement vector for the whole journey.

examples.derivation: The standard vector i points right, so -2i points 2 units left and has magnitude 2. The standard vector j points up, so 3j points 3 units up and has magnitude 3. These directions meet at 90 degrees. The diagram endpoints and right-angle marker agree. Source basis-vector definitions, negative-vector teaching and component-form sketch activities support the method.

The endpoint differences are p=(-1,0), q=(0,1) and r=(3,0), giving lengths 1, 1 and 3 grid units. Thus p and q are unit vectors and r is not. The question supplies the scale and all required givens without revealing classifications. Source geometric-length interpretation and unit-vector identification support this method.

The supplied magnitudes are 1 and 0.6. Applying the source definition directly identifies u as a unit vector and excludes v. Neither direction changes this criterion. A diagram is unnecessary because both magnitudes are explicitly supplied.

Magnitude 0 identifies z as the zero vector, which has no direction. Since 0 differs from 1, z is not a unit vector. These conclusions follow directly from the supplied zero-vector and unit-vector definitions; no diagram or additional method is needed.

Subtracting 8c from itself gives the zero vector. The journey combines 4 km north with 4 km south, yielding zero displacement because the endpoints coincide. The separate diagram arrows have equal lengths and opposite directions, and the prose explicitly explains their separate placement. Source subtraction part d, displacement investigation and zero-vector teaching support the cancellation method. The aligned cancellation includes the required phantom equals gutter.
